questions.q: A village cricket club has a five-member committee. The committee fixes the monthly fee, decides the practice timings and removes members who do not pay. Using the chapter's words, what is the committee, and what is the work it does?
questions.a: The committee is like a government; its work is governance. It makes rules (the fee, the timings) and ensures they are followed (removing members who do not pay), so its work is more than making rules; and a club's rules are not laws, which are some of the more important rules of a government.
o: The committee is like a government; its work is governance
The committee is the governance; its work is the government
The committee is like a government; its work is only making rules
The committee's rules are laws; its work is governance

questions.q:
Read the statements about rules as the chapter describes them.
1. A housing colony of 500 families needs rules mainly because a large number of people live there together.
2. A school's rule that teachers must sign in by 8 am is a law, because many people have to follow it.
3. A rule can still be changed after it is made, for example when the people it binds ask for a change.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 1 is correct: when a large number of people live together there can be disagreements and disorder, so rules become necessary. Statement 3 is correct: rules are not set once and for all; a student body might ask the management to change a rule. Statement 2 is wrong: the number of people who follow a rule does not make it a law; laws are some of the more important rules made by a government.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Ravi says: 'Rules are only useful for punishing people. A town would run just as well if nobody followed any rule.' Which point from the chapter answers him directly?
questions.a: If no one followed rules, society could not function
o: If no one followed rules, society could not function
Some of the more important rules are called laws
Citizens have a say in the laws governing society
Rules and laws, once they are made, stay fixed for all time

questions.q:
A pupil writes: 'If everyone in a country were honest and kind, the country could run without any government.'
(a) Describe one situation among honest, kind people in which a disagreement could still arise if there were no rule.
(b) Use the chapter's reason why rules become necessary to judge the pupil's claim.
questions.a: (a) Any fitting situation, for example: two honest families in a colony both want the one community hall on the same Sunday, and with no rule on bookings they cannot settle who gets it. (b) The claim does not hold. The chapter says that when a large number of people live together there can be disagreements and disorder, so rules become necessary to keep order and harmony; this happens with honest people too, which is why its summary says no country can run without governance and government.
s: Part (a): a fitting disagreement among honest people with no rule
Part (b): claim rejected, because many people living together need rules and a government

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Going by the chapter, a home of four people has no rules, because rules are needed only where a large number of people live together.
Reason (R): When a large number of people live together, there can be disagreements and disorder.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. R is the chapter's own reason why rules become necessary in a society. But A stretches it too far: the chapter says there are probably some simple rules at home that you are expected to follow, so a small home has rules too.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Green Park Apartments in Hyderabad has 120 flats but only 90 parking slots. Last month the residents' committee met and voted on a rule: one car per flat inside the gates, and printed it on notices at both gates. A survey this month found that 70 of the 120 flats have read the rule. The committee received 14 complaints of cars blocking the gate; 12 of them were about cars from flats that had read the rule. Nobody checks cars at the gate. The committee has Rs 9,000 left this month: a guard to check cars costs Rs 8,500 a month, and fresh notices delivered to every flat cost Rs 2,000.
(a) Which two parts of the chapter's meaning of governance has the committee already carried out?
(b) How many flats have not read the rule, and how many of the 14 complaints came from flats that had read it?
(c) What do your numbers in (b) show about which part of governance is weakest here?
(d) The committee can afford only one spend this month. Which should it choose, and how much money will be left? Justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Taking a decision (the vote on the one-car rule) and organising the residents' life with that rule (the notices at the gates); either wording of these two parts earns the mark. (b) 120 - 70 = 50 flats have not read it; 12 of the 14 complaints came from flats that had read it, and only 14 - 12 = 2 from the others. (c) Not knowing the rule is not the main problem: most blocking is by people who know it. What is weak is the third part of governance, ensuring that the rule is followed. (d) The guard: 9,000 - 8,500 = Rs 500 left. The notices are cheaper (Rs 7,000 would be left) and would reach the 50 flats that have not read the rule, but those flats caused only 2 of the 14 complaints; a guard deals with the missing part, ensuring the rule is followed.
s: Part (a): taking a decision and organising life with the rule
Part (b): 50 flats unread; 12 of 14 complaints from flats that had read it
Part (c): the weak part is ensuring the rule is followed
Part (d): the guard, Rs 500 left, justified from the complaint numbers

questions.q:
A school's notice board shows three rules: (1) Phones may not be carried into the examination hall. (2) Teachers must sign the attendance register by 7:45 am. (3) Students must wear the school uniform on all working days.
(a) For each rule, say who has to follow it.
(b) A Class 6 pupil reads the board and says, 'School rules are only for students.' Use your answer to (a) and the chapter to correct her.
questions.a: (a) Rule 1: students appearing for the examination; Rule 2: teachers; Rule 3: students. (b) Her claim fails because Rule 2 binds teachers. The chapter says the school has rules too, some for students and others for teachers, so school rules are not only for students.
s: Part (a): exam candidates, teachers, students for the three rules
Part (b): rule 2 binds teachers; the chapter says school rules are for students and teachers

questions.q: At a bakery, the owner promised his 6 workers a weekly holiday when they joined, and the workers must wear hairnets because the owner's rule says so. Counting the owner too, the number of people at the bakery who are bound by a rule is ___ (write the number in digits).
Kabir argues: 'A law is a kind of rule. So every rule, even my family's rule about bedtime, is a law.' Check his claim against the chapter. Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The first half is right: a law is a rule. But the chapter says only some of the more important rules made by a government are called laws. A family's bedtime rule is made by parents at home, not by the government, so it is a rule but not a law. Kabir has turned 'every law is a rule' around into 'every rule is a law', which does not follow.
s: Verdict: No, the claim does not hold
Only some of the more important rules made by a government are called laws
A family rule is not made by the government, so the reversal 'every rule is a law' fails

questions.q: At a garment unit in Tiruppur, the owner promised the workers a half-day every Saturday when they joined, and the owner's rule says workers must wear a cap near the machines. One Saturday the owner keeps everyone till 8 pm, and the same day a worker comes without a cap. Going by the chapter, who has broken a rule?
questions.a: Both: the owner his promise, the worker the cap rule
o: Both: the owner his promise, the worker the cap rule
Only the worker, as an owner sets rules but is not bound
Only the owner, as a worker's cap rule is not a law
Neither, as workplace rules are not laws and do not bind

questions.q:
A new hostel for 300 students opens in a town with no rules at all: no meal timings, no lights-out time, no rules about visitors.
(a) Using the chapter, predict one kind of problem that is likely to arise.
(b) The warden says: 'Rules will make the hostel strict and the students unhappy, so I will make rules only after trouble starts.' Weigh his point against the chapter's reason for rules and give your judgement.
questions.a: (a) Disagreements and disorder, for example quarrels over meal times or noise at night, because when many people live together there can be disagreement and disorder. (b) He is right that rules ask students to give up some freedom, but the chapter says that when a large number of people live together, rules become necessary to maintain order and harmony; with 300 students sharing one building, waiting for trouble means living with disorder first. A few clear rules from the start are the better course. (A reasoned answer for waiting, if it still says rules will be needed, earns the mark.)
s: Part (a): disagreements or disorder, with a hostel example
Part (b): weighs freedom against order; rules are needed where many people live together

questions.q:
Read this extract from a school newsletter.
'This term the Student Council asked the management to move Sports Day from April to January, since April afternoons are too hot. After a meeting, the management agreed. The staff handbook was also updated: teachers must now reach school by 7:40 am. For the Class 10 board examination, the school reminded candidates that no phones are allowed in the hall. Finally, the Council asked for the canteen to stay open after school; the management said no, because no staff are free then.'
(a) In the Sports Day story, who is acting like the government of the school and who is acting like citizens? Explain using the chapter's meaning of government.
(b) Which idea of the chapter about rules and laws does the change of the Sports Day date show?
(c) A classmate says the canteen refusal shows that the Student Council has no say at all. Using the extract and the chapter, judge her view.
questions.a: (a) The management acts like the government: it is the group that makes the school's rules (Sports Day dates, the staff handbook) and ensures they are followed. The Student Council acts like citizens, who have a say in the rules governing them. (b) Rules are not set once and for all: a student body can ask the management to change a rule, as citizens have a say in the laws and rules governing society. (c) Her view does not hold. The Sports Day request was accepted, and the canteen request was heard and turned down for a stated reason. Having a say means being able to ask for a change and be heard, not winning every request.
s: Part (a): management as the government, the Council like citizens
Part (b): rules are not set once and for all; citizens have a say
Part (c): view rejected, using the accepted and the heard-but-refused requests

questions.q: A college has no principal. A seven-member council makes the hostel rules, and wardens appointed by the council see that the rules are followed. A new student says, 'This college has no government, because no single person is in charge.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: A government can be a group or a system, not one person
o: A government can be a group or a system, not one person
He is right: a government needs one person at its head
Only the wardens form the government, as they enforce rules
The council is only governance; it cannot be a government

questions.q: Fifty families in a village share one handpump, and there are often long queues and quarrels. Write a short situation (four or five sentences) in which a group of villagers acts as a 'government' for the handpump. Your situation must show: (i) the group taking a decision, (ii) the rule it organises the families' use with, and (iii) how the group ensures the rule is followed.
questions.a: Any situation that shows all three, for example: The families choose five people as a handpump committee. The committee meets and decides (i) that each lane will use the pump at a fixed hour. (ii) It writes the timetable on a board beside the pump: Lane 1 at 6 am, Lane 2 at 7 am, and so on. (iii) Two committee members take turns to stand at the pump and send anyone who comes out of turn to the back. The committee is acting as a government because it makes the rule and ensures it is followed.
s: Shows the group taking a decision
States a clear rule that organises the use of the pump
Shows how the rule is made sure of (enforced), so the group acts as a government

questions.q: Compare and analyse a rule made by parents at home (for example, 'homework before television') with a law made by a government (for example, a law against stealing money online). Cover (i) who makes each, (ii) why only one of them is called a law, (iii) one example from the chapter of how a government sees that a law is followed, (iv) how each can be changed, and (v) why the chapter says rules of every kind are needed.
questions.a: (i) The home rule is made by the parents; the law is made by the government, the group of individuals or the system that makes rules and ensures they are followed. (ii) Only some of the more important rules made by a government are called laws, so the home rule is a rule but not a law. (iii) Under the laws against cybercrime, criminals who steal money digitally have been arrested and convicted in court, and are usually fined and jailed for some years. (iv) A child can discuss a home rule with her parents; citizens likewise have a say in the laws and rules governing society, so neither is set once and for all. (v) When a large number of people live together there can be disagreements and disorder, so rules are needed to keep order and harmony; if no one followed rules, society would not be able to function.
s: (i) Makers: parents versus the government
(ii) Only the more important rules of a government are laws
(iii) Arrest, conviction, fine and jail under cybercrime laws
(iv) Discussing with parents versus citizens having a say
(v) Rules keep order where many people live together

questions.q: True or False? 'A rule that the State government makes, fining shops that sell expired medicines, could be called a law, but a school's rule on uniforms could not.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says some of the more important rules made by a government are called laws. The fine on expired medicines is a rule made by the State government for the whole society, so it can be a law; the uniform rule is made by a school for its own students, so it is a rule but not a law.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: laws are some of the more important rules made by a government; a school rule is not made by a government

questions.q: A Class 6 group lists the settings the chapter's opening paragraph uses to show that rules are everywhere. Which entry on their list does NOT come from that paragraph?
questions.a: Rules for people watching a film in a cinema hall
o: Rules for people watching a film in a cinema hall
Rules that teachers in a school must follow
Rules that drivers on the road are expected to obey
Rules that students follow in examinations

questions.q: Karan says: 'Every law is a rule, but not every rule is a law. My school's rule on uniforms is a rule, yet it is not a law.' Check his claim against the chapter. Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says some of the more important rules are called laws, so every law is one kind of rule. But only some of the more important rules made by a government are laws, so many rules are not laws. The school's uniform rule is made by the school for its students, not by the government, so it is a rule but not a law. Karan has the relation the right way round.
s: Verdict: Yes, the claim holds
Laws are some of the more important rules, so every law is a rule
The uniform rule is the school's, not a government's, so it is not a law

questions.q:
A city's diary records how it handled a new rule for e-rickshaws.
2 January: Many complaints arrive about overloaded e-rickshaws causing disorder on the roads.
10 January: The city council decides that an e-rickshaw may carry no more than four passengers.
15 January: The rule is announced, and stands and fares are reorganised around it.
From 1 February: Officials check e-rickshaws on the roads and stop those that break the rule.
1 August, after six months of the rule: Drivers' groups ask the city to change one part of the rule.
For each of the five dated entries, say which idea from the chapter it shows. Then explain why the 1 August entry does not mean the city's governance has failed.
questions.a: 2 January: disorder among many people sharing the roads shows why rules become necessary to keep order and harmony. 10 January: taking a decision, the first part of governance. 15 January: organising society's life with the rule, the second part. From 1 February: ensuring the rule is followed, the third part, which is what makes the city council act as a government. 1 August: citizens have a say in the rules governing them. This is not a failure: the chapter says rules and laws are not set once and for all, so a request to change a rule after it has been in force is part of how governance works. (The 2 January entry may also be read as citizens having a say, since the complaints come from the public; accept it with that reason.)
s: 2 January: disorder shows the need for rules
10 January: taking a decision
15 January: organising life with the rule
1 February: ensuring the rule is followed
1 August: citizens' say; rules are not set once and for all, so not a failure

questions.q: True or False? A student writes in her notes: 'In our school, the management is the governance, and running the school by rules is the government.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. She has swapped the two words. The management, the group that makes the school's rules and ensures they are followed, acts like the government; the work of taking decisions, organising school life with rules and ensuring they are followed is governance.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the management is like the government; running the school by rules is governance

questions.q:
Read the statements about the organs of government.
1. The executive includes the head of state and the ministers, but not the police.
2. The judiciary can examine whether a law passed by the legislature is fair to all.
3. The legislature can remove an existing law.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. Statement 2 is correct: the judiciary sometimes examines whether a law passed by the legislature is well conceived and fair to all. Statement 3 is correct: the legislature sometimes updates or removes existing laws. Statement 1 is wrong: the executive also includes any agency responsible for law and order, such as the cyber police.
o: 2 and 3 only
3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: After arresting a man for snatching a chain at a bus stop, a police officer tells reporters: 'The State law allows up to three years in jail, and I have decided he will get the full three years.' Going by the chapter, which organ's work has she stepped into, and which part of what she did is still her own organ's job?
questions.a: The judiciary's; the arrest is still her organ's job
o: The judiciary's; the arrest is still her organ's job
The legislature's; the arrest is a court's job
No organ's; police may fix any term the law allows
The judiciary's; the arrest is the legislature's job

questions.q:
A State Assembly passes a law that weekly markets may stay open until 9 pm. A week later, a district office orders all market shops to close at 8 pm instead, saying the law 'needed a small change'.
(a) Which organ made the law, and which organ does the district office belong to?
(b) Which organ has gone beyond its expected role? Explain using what each organ is meant to do.
questions.a: (a) The legislature (the State Assembly) made the law; the district office is part of the executive. (b) The executive has gone beyond its role. Its job is to implement (execute) the law as made; changing or updating a law is the work of the legislature. Under the separation of powers, such an overstep can be checked and balance restored.
s: Part (a): legislature made the law; the district office is the executive
Part (b): the executive overstepped, since updating a law is the legislature's job

questions.q: A large village elects 15 people who meet to make the rules for its weekly market. A team of 3 officers checks the stalls, and one respected elder settles disputes over whether a stall broke a rule. Which of these is most like the legislature, and why?
questions.a: The 15 elected people: representatives making rules
o: The 15 elected people: representatives making rules
The 3 officers: they put the market rules into effect
The elder: he decides whether a stall broke a rule
The 15 elected people: they settle market disputes

questions.q:
A school is planning a Student Parliament with three groups: a Rules Group that writes school rules, an Action Group that makes sure the rules are followed, and a Fairness Court that decides whether a student has broken a rule and what should happen. Last term one group of five trusted prefects did all three jobs. They handled 30 cases; 28 went smoothly, but in 2 cases a student complained that the prefects had punished her under a rule they had written that same morning, and there was no one else to look into it. Keeping three groups needs 3 meetings a week; one group needs only 1.
(a) Which organ of a government does each of the three groups resemble?
(b) Which idea of the chapter explains why no one could look into the 2 complaints last term?
(c) If the jobs are split, which group could look into such a complaint, and what could it examine?
(d) Should the school split the jobs among three groups, even at 3 meetings a week? Decide, using (b) and (c) and the numbers.
questions.a: (a) Rules Group: legislature; Action Group: executive; Fairness Court: judiciary. (b) Separation of powers: with all three jobs in one group there were no checks and balances, so no one could check the group or restore balance when it acted beyond its role. (c) The Fairness Court, kept separate, could decide whether the student really broke a rule and could also examine whether the rule was fair and whether the Action Group acted rightly. (d) Yes, split them. One group was quicker and 28 of 30 cases went well, but in the other 2 there was no remedy at all; the chapter says that in good governance the three organs must be kept separate so that each can check the others, and two extra meetings a week is the cost of that check. (A reasoned answer for keeping one group earns the mark for (d) only if it deals with the 2 cases that had no check.)
s: Part (a): legislature, executive, judiciary
Part (b): no separation of powers, so no checks and balances
Part (c): the Fairness Court, examining the case and the fairness of the rule or action
Part (d): split the jobs, weighing 28 smooth cases and fewer meetings against 2 cases with no check

questions.q: A State Assembly keeps its old law on fireworks but changes it so that the fine for bursting crackers after 10 pm is higher. Which organ is at work, and which of its jobs is this?
questions.a: The legislature, updating an existing law
o: The legislature, updating an existing law
The executive, implementing an existing law
The legislature, removing an existing law
The judiciary, deciding the punishment

questions.q: True or False? 'When a court fines a shopkeeper for selling fake medicines under a State law, the court did not make that law, yet deciding the shopkeeper's punishment is the court's own job.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The law was made by the legislature, the organ that makes new laws. The court is part of the judiciary, the system of courts that decides whether someone has broken the law and, if so, what action should follow, including punishment.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the legislature made the law; the judiciary decides guilt and the punishment

questions.q: A news story about forged land records names six people or bodies: the Chief Minister, the Revenue Minister, the State police, the cyber police unit that traced the forgers, a judge, and the State Assembly that passed the land-records law. Sorted into the three organs of government, the largest group holds ___ of them (write the number in digits).

Create a short situation (three or four sentences) about a new rule on plastic bags in a city. Your situation must show each of the three organs doing a job the chapter gives it, and one of the jobs must be the judiciary examining something another organ has done.
questions.a: Any situation meeting all conditions, for example: The State Assembly passes a law banning thin plastic bags (legislature makes a law). City officers and police inspect shops and seize banned bags (executive implements the law). A shopkeeper goes to court saying officers sealed his shop without checking; the court examines whether the officers' decision was right and orders the seal removed (judiciary examining an executive decision).
s: Legislature makes or updates the law
Executive implements or enforces it
Judiciary examines an executive decision or the law's fairness

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In a system of good governance, the legislature, the executive and the judiciary are kept separate.
Reason (R): When the organs are separate, each can check what the others are doing and restore balance if one acts beyond its expected role.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter says the three organs must be kept separate (the separation of powers), and that this separation is intended to provide a system of checks and balances, which is exactly what R describes.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: In a story, a king makes all the laws and alone decides who is guilty and how they are punished, while his soldiers arrest anyone who breaks his laws. Going by the chapter, which organs does each stand for, and what is missing?
questions.a: King: legislature and judiciary; soldiers: executive; no separate court
o: King: legislature and judiciary; soldiers: executive; no separate court
King: the executive only; soldiers: the judiciary; there is no legislature
King: legislature and judiciary; soldiers: executive; there is no executive
King: the judiciary only; soldiers: legislature; no separate court

questions.q: In the imaginary town of Nayapur, one group of five people makes the laws, runs the police and also acts as the only court. Yesterday the group passed a law banning street stalls; today its police arrested a fruit seller, and its court jailed her the same afternoon. Analyse how Nayapur would work differently if it followed the chapter's separation of powers.
questions.a: 1. Making the law would be the job of the legislature, an assembly of representatives of the people, not of the group that also runs the police. 2. Arresting the fruit seller would be the job of the executive, which implements laws through an agency responsible for law and order. 3. Whether she actually broke the law, and what action or punishment should follow, would be decided by a separate judiciary, a system of courts. 4. The judiciary could also examine whether the law banning stalls is well conceived and fair to all, and whether the executive's action was right. 5. Because the three organs would be separate, each could check what the others do and restore balance if one acted beyond its role; in Nayapur nobody can check the group.
s: Law made by a legislature of representatives
Arrest by the executive's law-and-order agency
Guilt and punishment decided by separate courts
Courts able to examine the law's fairness and the executive's action
Checks and balances: each organ can check the others, unlike in Nayapur

questions.q: True or False? 'Because the legislature is an assembly of representatives of the people, it can also arrest the people who break the laws it makes.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The legislature makes, updates or removes laws. Arresting people who break a law is the work of the executive, through an agency responsible for law and order such as the police; deciding whether they broke the law is the judiciary's work.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the legislature makes laws; the executive's law-and-order agency arrests

questions.q:
A State tightens its road-safety rules. Match each event in Column A with what it shows in Column B.
Column A: 1. The Assembly passes a law making helmets compulsory for pillion riders  2. Traffic police stop riders without helmets and book them  3. A court hears a rider's case and decides that he broke the law and must pay a fine  4. A court looks at the helmet law itself and finds that one of its fines is not fair to all
Column B: a. the legislature making a new law  b. the executive enforcing law and order  c. the judiciary deciding a case and the action to follow  d. the judiciary examining whether a law is fair to all
questions.a: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d. The Assembly legislates; the traffic police are the law-and-order agency of the executive; in event 3 the court decides whether one person broke the law and what follows, while in event 4 it examines whether the law passed by the legislature is fair to all, the judiciary's other job.

questions.q:
Study this timeline of an illegal sand-mining case in a State.
Jan 2025: The State Assembly passes a law against taking sand from rivers without a permit.
Mar 2026: The river police arrest a contractor for 40 truckloads of sand taken without a permit.
Mar 2026: The police chief orders that the boats of all fishermen on that river be seized too.
Apr 2026: A court rules that seizing the fishermen's boats was not right and cancels the order.
Jul 2026: A court finds the contractor guilty and fines him Rs 3,000 for each truckload, plus jail.
(a) Name the organ at work in each of the five entries.
(b) Which entry shows an organ going beyond its expected role, and which entry restores the balance?
(c) What is the contractor's total fine?
(d) A reader writes that the court 'interfered' in April and should only punish criminals. Is the reader right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Jan 2025: legislature; both Mar 2026 entries: executive (river police and police chief); Apr 2026 and Jul 2026: judiciary. (b) The police chief's order to seize the fishermen's boats goes beyond the executive's role; the court's April ruling cancels it and restores balance. (c) 40 x Rs 3,000 = Rs 1,20,000. (d) No. The chapter says the judiciary sometimes examines whether a decision taken by the executive is right; under checks and balances each organ can check what another is doing and restore balance if one acts beyond its role. Punishing law-breakers is only one part of its work.
s: Part (a): legislature; executive twice; judiciary twice
Part (b): the order to seize the boats oversteps; the April ruling restores balance
Part (d): not right; the judiciary may examine executive decisions (checks and balances)

questions.q:
After several road accidents, a court announces a new rule of its own: no two-wheeler may be driven above 40 km per hour anywhere in the State.
(a) Which organ's job is the court doing here?
(b) What does the chapter say a court may do about laws instead? Give both of its jobs that involve laws.
questions.a: (a) The legislature's: making a new law is the work of the legislature, an assembly of representatives of the people, not of the courts. (b) The judiciary decides whether someone has broken a law and what action, including punishment, should follow; and it can examine whether a law passed by the legislature is well conceived and fair to all.
s: Part (a): the court is making a law, the legislature's job
Part (b): decide whether a law was broken and the action; examine whether a law is fair

questions.q:
Thirty years ago, people in India sent money to a distant relative by money order from the Post Office; today it can be sent digitally in seconds.
(a) Using the chapter, explain why this change led many governments to pass new laws.
(b) Which organ passes such laws, and why could the cyber police not simply make such a law themselves?
questions.a: (a) Digital ways of sending money also created a new class of criminals who steal people's money digitally without leaving their desks; to fight such criminal activities, called cybercrime, governments passed new laws. (b) The legislature, the organ that makes new laws. The cyber police belong to the executive, whose job is to implement laws; under the separation of powers the organs are kept separate, so the executive does not make the laws it enforces.
s: Part (a): digital money brought a new kind of crime (cybercrime), so new laws were passed to fight it
Part (b): the legislature; the cyber police are the executive, which implements laws and is kept separate

questions.q: Suppose a State's legislature passes a law that only people living in the State capital may apply for jobs in State government offices. Using the chapter, explain (i) which organ could examine this law, (ii) what question it would ask about the law, and (iii) which idea of the chapter this shows in action.
questions.a: (i) The judiciary, the system of courts. (ii) The chapter says the judiciary sometimes examines whether a law passed by the legislature is well conceived and fair to all; here it would ask whether a law that shuts out people outside the capital is fair to all. (iii) Checks and balances under the separation of powers: one organ (the judiciary) checks what another (the legislature) has done and can restore balance if it went beyond its expected role.
s: (i) The judiciary
(ii) Whether the law is well conceived and fair to all
(iii) Checks and balances: one organ checking another

questions.q: Anika says: 'Separation of powers means the legislature, the executive and the judiciary never deal with each other at all.' Check her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the three organs must be kept separate, although they interact with each other and work together. In the cybercrime example the legislature passed the law, the executive (cyber police) arrested the criminals under it and the courts convicted them, so all three were part of one chain. Separate means each keeps its own role, not that they never meet; the separation also lets each organ check what the others are doing.
s: Verdict: No
The organs are separate but interact and work together
Evidence: the cybercrime chain, or each organ checking the others

questions.q: Your aunt in Mysuru lost Rs 18,000 when she clicked a fake payment link. Write a short letter to her explaining how each organ of government plays its part in her case, how the three depend on one another, and why it matters that they are still kept separate.
questions.a: 1. The legislature has made laws against cybercrime: many governments passed new laws because criminals found digital ways of stealing people's money. 2. The executive, through the cyber police (the agency responsible for law and order), can act on her complaint, trace the criminal and arrest him. 3. The judiciary, the system of courts, will decide whether the person broke the law and what punishment follows; such criminals are usually fined and jailed for some years. 4. The three depend on one another: the police can act only under a law the legislature has made, and the punishment is fixed by the court, not by the police. 5. They are still kept separate (separation of powers) so that there are checks and balances: each organ can check what the others are doing and restore balance if one acts beyond its role.
s: Legislature: laws against cybercrime
Executive: cyber police act and arrest
Judiciary: decides guilt and punishment (fine and jail)
The organs depend on one another: law first, then arrest, then the court's decision
Kept separate for checks and balances

questions.q: 'The three organs of government must be kept separate, although they interact with each other and work together.' Justify both halves of this statement. Use the cybercrime example for the second half.
questions.a: Separate: (1) the legislature makes, updates or removes laws through an assembly of representatives; (2) the executive, including the head of state, ministers and agencies such as the cyber police, implements the laws; (3) the judiciary, the system of courts, decides whether a law has been broken and what action follows. Keeping these apart is the separation of powers, which provides checks and balances: each organ can check the others and restore balance if one acts beyond its role. Working together: (4) in the cybercrime example, governments passed new laws against cybercrime, the cyber police acted under those laws and arrested criminals, and the courts convicted them, fining and jailing them; (5) no single organ could have dealt with the crime alone, which shows they interact as one chain.
s: Role of the legislature stated
Role of the executive stated
Role of the judiciary and the checks-and-balances purpose of keeping them separate
Cybercrime chain: law, arrest, conviction
Conclusion: no organ could act alone, so they work together

questions.q: The Kerala State Assembly passes a new law on fishing boats. A student must describe this in the chapter's terms, naming both the level of government and the organ of government at work. Which description is correct?
questions.a: State level; the legislature
o: State level; the legislature
State level; the executive
National level; the legislature
Legislature level; the State organ

questions.q:
Read the statements about the levels of government.
1. A flood in one part of a district that is not too severe may be dealt with by the local authorities without the State Government.
2. In the chapter's bulb comparison, checking the bulb, calling an electrician and complaining to the Electricity Board are three levels of dealing with a problem.
3. Apart from India, democratic countries have government at only one level.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. Statement 1 is correct: if a flood is not too severe, the local authorities may be able to deal with it. Statement 2 is correct: the chapter calls these three levels of dealing with a problem. Statement 3 is wrong: any democratic government operates at multiple levels, and in many countries, including India, it functions at three.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A diagram shows India's levels of government as a pyramid: local government (at the town or village level) is the base, the State government (at the State level) is the middle layer, and the Central government (at the national level) is the top.
(i) The handpump in one village breaks. At which layer would this most likely be dealt with first, and why?
(ii) If that layer could not cope, which layers lie above it, in order?
(iii) Where does the chapter place ordinary citizens with respect to this pyramid, and what does grassroots democracy let them do?
questions.a: (i) The base, local government: the problem is small and lies in one village, the town or village level at which local government works, and the chapter shows problems being dealt with first at the closest level. (ii) The State government, then the Central government. (iii) The chapter calls ordinary citizens the base of the pyramid; grassroots democracy enables and encourages their participation, so they can have a say in decisions which affect them.
s: (i) Local government first, since the problem is in one village
(ii) State government, then Central government
(iii) Citizens are the base; grassroots democracy gives them a say in decisions affecting them

questions.q: After a storm, a fallen tree blocks the only road into one village; no other place is affected. A villager says, 'Only the Central Government can clear our road.' Going by how the chapter says problems are handled at different levels, who would most likely deal with this first?
questions.a: The local authorities of that village area
o: The local authorities of that village area
The Central Government, sending the army
The State Government, sending rescue teams
The High Court, deciding who is to blame

questions.q:
(a) Asha lives in Bengaluru. Using the chapter's three levels, how many levels of government is she governed by at the same time? Name them.
(b) Her cousin in a small village says, 'I live in a village, so fewer levels of government work for me.' Correct him.
questions.a: (a) Three: the local government of her town (city), the State government and the Central government. (b) The local level works at the town or village level, so a village also has local government; above it are the same State and Central governments. He too is governed at all three levels.
s: Part (a): three levels named (local, State, Central)
Part (b): local government works at the town or village level, so the village also has all three levels

questions.q:
In one monsoon week, a State receives three flood reports.
Report P: In one part of District P, 2 villages are flooded; the water is not deep and is already going down.
Report Q: In District Q, 4 towns and 60 villages are under water.
Report R: Floods cover vast areas across 9 districts, cutting off roads and food supplies.
The State has 10 rescue teams. Report Q needs 6 teams and Report R needs 8, and each need must be met in full. Following the chapter, the Central Government comes to help only in a massive flood affecting vast areas.
(a) Which report can the local authorities most likely handle on their own, and why?
(b) In which report does the chapter expect the State Government to step in with rescue teams, while the Central Government is not needed?
(c) For which report alone can the State ask the Central Government for help, and what kinds of help may it send?
(d) How should the State share its 10 teams between Q and R, and how many teams must it ask the Centre for? Show why any other split leaves a need that no one can meet.
questions.a: (a) Report P: the flood is in one part of a district and not too severe, so the local authorities may deal with it. (b) Report Q: it involves several towns and many villages, so the State Government steps in and sends rescue teams. (c) Report R, a massive flood affecting vast areas: the Central Government may also come to help by sending relief supplies, the army and so on. (d) 6 teams to Q and 10 - 6 = 4 to R; R still needs 8 - 4 = 4 more teams' worth of help, which the State asks the Centre for (the Centre may send the army and relief supplies). Any split giving Q fewer than 6 (for example 2 to Q and 8 to R) leaves Q short, and Q is not a massive flood, so the Centre would not come for it; only R's shortfall can be met from the Centre.
s: Part (a): Report P, not too severe, local authorities
Part (b): Report Q, several towns and many villages
Part (c): Report R only; relief supplies and the army
Part (d): 6 to Q, 4 to R, ask the Centre for 4, since Q's shortfall cannot go to the Centre

questions.q: Asked to name the three levels of government in India, a student writes: 'the Supreme Court, the High Court and the local court'. What has the student mixed up?
questions.a: She named courts, not local, State and Central
o: She named courts, not local, State and Central
She named the three organs instead of the three levels
She named levels of the legislature, not of government
She named the national level but left out the local one

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In a massive flood affecting vast areas, the Central Government may also come to help.
Reason (R): The Central Government forms the base of the chapter's pyramid of three levels.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. A is true: the chapter says the Central Government may send relief supplies and the army in a massive flood. R is false: the local government, at the town or village level, forms the base; the Central Government is at the national level, at the top.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
The chapter teaches the levels with two examples: the bulb that will not light up and the flood.
(a) Give one way the two examples are alike.
(b) Give one way in which they are different, and say which of the two uses the actual levels of government in India.
questions.a: (a) Any valid likeness, for example: in both, a problem is dealt with at three levels, starting with the closest and moving up only if it is too big for the lower one. (b) Any valid difference, for example: the bulb's levels are you, an electrician and the Electricity Board, which are not governments, or the bulb is a problem in one home while the flood affects whole areas. The flood example uses the actual levels: the local authorities, the State Government and the Central Government.
s: Part (a): a valid likeness
Part (b): a valid difference, and the flood example named as using the real levels

questions.q:
The chapter gives two mottos: Satyameva Jayate ('Truth alone triumphs'), the Government of India's motto, and Yato Dharmastato Jayah ('Where there is dharma, there is victory'), the Supreme Court's motto.
(a) A designer proposes putting Satyameva Jayate on a new wing of the Supreme Court, saying 'the Supreme Court is part of the government, so it should carry the government's motto.' Using the chapter, what should go on the new wing, and what is weak in the designer's reasoning?
(b) Explain how the meaning of the Supreme Court's motto suits the work the chapter gives the judiciary.
questions.a: (a) Yato Dharmastato Jayah, because the chapter gives it as the Supreme Court's own motto. The designer is right that the judiciary is an organ of government, but the chapter gives the court an institution motto of its own, so being part of the government does not mean using the Government of India's motto. (b) The judiciary decides whether someone has broken the law and what should follow, and examines whether a decision or a law is right and fair to all; a motto saying victory lies where dharma (what is right) is fits a body whose work is to decide what is right and lawful.
s: Part (a): Yato Dharmastato Jayah on the wing; the court has its own motto although it is an organ of government
Part (b): the motto's link between dharma and victory tied to the judiciary deciding what is lawful and fair

questions.q: A diagram of India's levels of government is a pyramid of three layers: local government at the town or village level forms the base, the State government at the State level is the middle layer, and the Central government at the national level is the top. A flood in one part of a district that is not too severe is first dealt with at one of these layers. The number of layers above that layer is ___ (write the number in digits).

A hill district keeps a log after a cloudburst.
Day 1: a small landslide blocks the road into one village; the district's 1 rescue team clears it by evening.
Day 3: fresh landslides cut off 5 towns and 70 villages; the State sends 7 of its 12 rescue teams.
Day 6: landslides spread over vast areas of several districts; army trucks with relief supplies sent by the Central Government arrive.
On Day 1 a village leader had asked the State to send all 12 of its teams to his village at once, 'just in case'.
(a) Which level of government most likely dealt with Day 1, and why?
(b) Why did the State step in on Day 3, going by the chapter?
(c) Should the State's teams have gone home when the army arrived on Day 6? Explain.
(d) Judge the village leader's Day 1 request.
questions.a: (a) The local authorities: the problem was in one village and not too severe, the kind the chapter says local authorities may deal with. (b) It now involved several towns and many villages, which is when the chapter says the State Government steps in and sends rescue teams. (c) No: in a disaster over vast areas the Central Government may also come to help, so it joins the State and local efforts rather than replacing them. (d) The request was unwise. The chapter's levels deal with a problem first at the closest level and bring in a higher level only when the problem grows beyond it; a blocked road in one village is a local matter, and the district's 1 team cleared it the same day, so 11 extra teams were not needed. Sending all 12 State teams to one village would also have taken them away from the rest of the State that day. (A reasoned answer in favour of caution earns the mark only if it shows why a one-village problem needed the State.)
s: Part (a): local authorities, one village and not severe
Part (b): several towns and many villages bring in the State
Part (c): no, the Centre also helps; it does not replace the others
Part (d): request unwise; a one-village problem is first handled locally, and 1 team was enough

questions.q:
A water pipe bursts in one lane of a town. Months later, a drought leaves many towns and villages across a whole State short of water.
(a) Using the chapter's idea that each level deals with different matters, which level of government would you most likely expect to deal with each problem?
(b) Why would it make little sense to take the burst pipe in one lane straight to the Central Government?
questions.a: (a) The burst pipe: the local government, which works at the town or village level. The State-wide shortage: the State Government, which works at the State level and steps in when many towns and villages are hit. (b) The Central Government works at the national level; a problem in one lane is small and local, and the chapter shows problems being dealt with first at the closest level, moving up only when a lower level cannot cope.
s: Part (a): lane pipe to the local level; State-wide shortage to the State level
Part (b): the Centre works at the national level; small problems go to the closest level first

questions.q: One news report speaks of 'the Union government', a second of 'the Central Government', and a third of 'the government at the national level'. A reader thinks the reports are about three different governments. Going by the chapter, what is true?
questions.a: All three name the same top level of government
o: All three name the same top level of government
They are the local, State and national levels
'Union' and 'Central' differ; 'national' is a third
Only 'national level' is a level of government

questions.q: Lakshmi says: 'The local government looks after my village and the Central government looks after the nation, so the State government has nothing to do with my life.' How far is she right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half matches the chapter: the local government works at the town or village level and the Central government at the national level. The second half is wrong: each level deals with different matters, and the State level has its own. The chapter's table gives the State government functions such as police, law and order, public health and education, and when a flood involves several towns and many villages the State Government steps in with rescue teams. So the State government touches her life too.
s: Verdict: partly right
Correct half: local at town or village level, Central at national level
Wrong half: the State has its own matters (police, public health, education; rescue teams in a wide flood)

questions.q:
A cyclone is forecast for a coastal region. Three warnings are issued.
Warning 1: strong winds may damage a few huts in one fishing village.
Warning 2: heavy rain and flooding are likely in 5 towns and 80 villages of two districts.
Warning 3: a severe cyclone may strike vast areas along the coast, cutting roads and food supplies.
Using the chapter's account of how the three levels deal with a flood, analyse (i) which level would most likely deal with Warning 1, (ii) which level would step in for Warning 2 and with what, (iii) which level may also come in for Warning 3 and with what, (iv) whether the lower levels stop working once the higher one arrives, and (v) why one level alone could not be expected to handle all three warnings.
questions.a: (i) The local authorities, since the problem is in one village and not too severe. (ii) The State Government, which steps in with rescue teams when several towns and many villages are affected. (iii) The Central Government, which may also come to help by sending relief supplies, the army and so on, when vast areas are affected. (iv) No: the chapter says the Centre may 'also' come to help, so it joins the State and local efforts rather than replacing them. (v) Each level deals with different matters and works at a different place (town or village, State, nation), so problems of different sizes are shared out among the three levels instead of all going to one.
s: (i) Local authorities for one village
(ii) State Government with rescue teams for several towns and villages
(iii) Central Government may also send relief and the army for vast areas
(iv) Higher levels join, not replace, the lower ones
(v) Each level deals with different matters, so no single level handles all

questions.q: Going by the chapter's idea that each level of government deals with different matters, which of these would NOT be dealt with first by the local government of a town or village?
questions.a: Talks with another country about a border
o: Talks with another country about a border
A choked drain in one lane of a town
A broken streetlight on one village lane
A leaking tap at the only well in a small village

questions.q: Raju says: 'By the chapter's bulb comparison, the first thing to do when a bulb does not light up is to file a complaint with the Electricity Board.' Show that the comparison cannot mean this, and say what the same logic means for how a problem moves between the levels of government.
questions.a: In the chapter's comparison you first check the bulb, switch and fuse yourself; only if that fails do you call an electrician; and only if the problem is found not to be within your home do you go to the Electricity Board. So the Board is the last step, not the first. In the same way, a problem is first dealt with at the level closest to it, the local government, and the State and then the Centre come in only as it grows beyond what the lower level can manage.
s: States the chapter's order: self-check, electrician, Board
Shows the Board comes in only when the fault is outside the home
Applies the same logic: a problem goes first to the closest level and moves up only as it grows

questions.q: Your cousin in Class 4 asks, 'Why does India need three tiers of government? Wouldn't one big government be simpler?' Write a reply that answers her, using the chapter's flood example and its bulb comparison, and ending with your own judgement on her 'simpler' idea.
questions.a: 1. The chapter says any democratic government operates at multiple levels, and India works at three: local, State and Central. 2. Each level deals with different matters, and works at a different place: the town or village, the State, and the nation. 3. Problems come in different sizes, as in the bulb comparison: you check the bulb, switch and fuse yourself first, call an electrician next, and go to the Electricity Board only if the fault is outside your home. 4. A flood works the same way: local authorities can handle a small one, the State sends rescue teams when several towns and many villages are hit, and the Centre may send relief supplies and the army in a massive flood over vast areas. 5. So one big government at the top would be like calling the Electricity Board about every bulb: three tiers let each problem be handled at the level that suits it.
s: Three levels named: local, State, Central
Each level deals with different matters at a different place
Bulb comparison used correctly
Flood example used for all three levels
Conclusion: each problem is handled at the level that suits it

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter says the local, State and Central governments all deal with the same matters; they differ only in the size of the area they cover.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says each level deals with different matters, not the same ones; the local government works at the town or village level, the State government at the State level and the Central government at the national level.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: each level deals with different matters

questions.q:
Read the statements about the bodies in the chapter's table.
1. A State with two Houses has as many Houses in its legislature as the national level has.
2. A High Court is not a House, even though important decisions are made there.
3. A law for the whole country and a State's own law are formulated in different Houses.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3. Statement 1 is correct: a few States have two Houses, as the national level has two (the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha). Statement 2 is correct: a House is an assembly where laws are discussed or passed, and a High Court is a court of the judiciary. Statement 3 is correct: national laws are formulated by the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, a State's laws by its own State Assembly.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: A student is grouping bodies from the chapter's table by level. Which pair shows the legislature and the judiciary of the SAME level?
questions.a: The Vidhan Sabha and the High Court
o: The Vidhan Sabha and the High Court
The Lok Sabha and the High Court
The Vidhan Sabha and the Supreme Court
The Rajya Sabha and the High Court

questions.q:
A news anchor says: 'The Lok Sabha passed the new national currency law today, so the law is now made.'
(a) What does the chapter's table say about which bodies formulate national laws?
(b) Why would no State's Vidhan Sabha be involved in formulating this currency law?
questions.a: (a) National laws are formulated by two Houses, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, so the Lok Sabha is not the only House involved. (b) The Vidhan Sabha is the State Assembly at the State level; a law for the whole country is a national law, formulated by the legislature at the national level.
s: Part (a): both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha formulate national laws
Part (b): the Vidhan Sabha is a State-level assembly; national laws belong to the national legislature

questions.q:
Match each event in Column A with the body in Column B where it would take place, going by the chapter's table.
Column A: 1. Members debate a new currency law for the whole country  2. Members of a single-assembly State pass a law on agriculture for that State  3. The court at the State level examines whether an order of the State government was right  4. The court at the All India level examines whether a national law is fair to all
Column B: a. Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha  b. Vidhan Sabha  c. High Court  d. Supreme Court of India
questions.a: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d. National laws are formulated by the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha; a single-assembly State's laws by its Vidhan Sabha; the judiciary at the State level is the High Court and at the All India level the Supreme Court of India.

questions.q:
Meera made this chart of the chapter's table for her class wall.
Title: 'The Legislature and the Judiciary: where laws are carried out'
Judiciary | All India: High Court | State level: Supreme Court of India
Legislature | National level: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha | State level: always two Houses
(a) What is wrong in Meera's judiciary row? Correct it.
(b) What is wrong in her State-level legislature entry? Correct it.
(c) After the corrections, how many law-making Houses, at the national and State levels together, does the chart show for a State with a single assembly?
(d) Meera's title says these bodies are 'where laws are carried out'. Is this title right for the legislature? Judge it using the chapter's meaning of 'House' and what the legislature does.
questions.a: (a) The two courts are swapped: the Supreme Court of India is at the All India level and the High Court at the State level. (b) Not 'always two Houses': there is one State Assembly or Vidhan Sabha, and most States have a single assembly while a few have two. (c) 2 + 1 = 3 Houses (the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha and the State's Vidhan Sabha). (d) No. A House is an assembly where laws are discussed or passed, and the legislature makes, updates or removes laws; carrying out (implementing) laws is the executive's work. A better title: 'The Legislature and the Judiciary: where laws are made and judged'.
s: Part (a): Supreme Court at All India level, High Court at State level
Part (b): one State Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) in most States, a few with two
Part (c): 3 Houses
Part (d): wrong title; legislature discusses and passes laws, the executive carries them out

questions.q: A State needs a new law on irrigation for its farmers, and the country needs a new law on currency. A student says both laws should be passed by that State's Vidhan Sabha. Which correction fits the chapter's table?
questions.a: Currency: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; irrigation: Vidhan Sabha
o: Currency: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; irrigation: Vidhan Sabha
Both laws: the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha together
Currency: Supreme Court of India; irrigation: High Court
Currency: the Lok Sabha on its own; irrigation: the Vidhan Sabha

questions.q: True or False? 'The Supreme Court, being the highest court of India, also formulates national laws together with the Lok Sabha.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. National laws are formulated by the two Houses of the national legislature, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. The Supreme Court of India is the judiciary at the All India level; it is a court, not a House.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha formulate national laws; the Supreme Court is the judiciary

questions.q: Tanmay says: 'Every body in the chapter's table has a partner at the other level: the Supreme Court pairs with the High Court, the Lok Sabha with the Vidhan Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha with each State's second House.' How far is he right? Check his claim against the table.
questions.a: Partly right. The judiciary pair holds: the Supreme Court of India is at the All India level and the High Court at the State level. The legislature does not pair up one for one: at the national level two Houses, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, together formulate national laws, while at the State level there is one State Assembly or Vidhan Sabha in most States. Only a few States have two Houses, so most States have no second House to set beside the Rajya Sabha.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: Supreme Court at All India level pairs with the High Court at State level
Wrong part: two national Houses, but most States have a single assembly and only a few have two

questions.q: Ravi lives in one of the few States whose legislature has two Houses. Counting the national and State levels together, the laws that apply to him are formulated in ___ different Houses (write the number in digits).

A shopkeeper in a State is accused of breaking a State law on weights and measures.
(a) Which court does the chapter's table place in the judiciary at the State level?
(b) A friend says the shopkeeper should ask the State's Vidhan Sabha to decide whether he broke the law. Explain why that is the wrong body.
questions.a: (a) The High Court. (b) The Vidhan Sabha is a House, an assembly where laws are discussed or passed, part of the legislature. Deciding whether someone has broken a law is the work of the judiciary, the system of courts.
s: Part (a): the High Court, the State-level judiciary in the table
Part (b): the Vidhan Sabha is a law-making House; deciding guilt is the courts' work

questions.q: A news report says a new law was 'passed by both Houses of the legislature'. A reader concludes that it must be a national law. Going by the chapter's table, why can she not be sure?
questions.a: A few States also have two Houses
o: A few States also have two Houses
Courts are also counted as Houses
National laws need only one House
Every State's legislature has two Houses

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha are both called Houses, but the Supreme Court of India is not.
Reason (R): A House is an assembly where laws are discussed or passed.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha formulate national laws, so they are assemblies where laws are discussed or passed; the Supreme Court is the judiciary at the All India level, a court that does not pass laws, so by the meaning of 'House' in R it is not one.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The imaginary State of Nilgiripur is one of the few States whose legislature has two Houses. One citizen of Nilgiripur thinks a new national law on communications is unfair to people in hill areas; another thinks a new State law on farm tax is unfair. Analyse, using the chapter's table and what it says about the organs: (i) which bodies formulated the national law, (ii) which body formulated the State law and how Nilgiripur differs from most States here, (iii) which court the table places at Nilgiripur's level and which at the All India level, (iv) which organ can examine whether a law is fair to all, and (v) why neither citizen can ask a House to judge the law the way a court does.
questions.a: (i) The two Houses of the national legislature, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, which formulate national laws. (ii) Nilgiripur's own State legislature, which has two Houses, whereas most States have a single assembly (the Vidhan Sabha). (iii) The High Court at the State level and the Supreme Court of India at the All India level. (iv) The judiciary: the chapter says it sometimes examines whether a law passed by the legislature is well conceived and fair to all. (v) A House is an assembly where laws are discussed or passed, part of the legislature that makes laws; judging whether a law is fair is the work of the courts, a separate organ, so that one organ can check another.
s: (i) Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha for the national law
(ii) Nilgiripur's two-House legislature, unlike most States' single assembly
(iii) High Court at State level, Supreme Court at All India level
(iv) The judiciary examines whether a law is fair to all
(v) Houses discuss or pass laws; courts judge them, as a separate organ

questions.q:
The chapter's table heads its judiciary row 'All India' and 'State level', but its legislature row 'National level' and 'State level'.
(a) Do 'All India' and 'National level' stand for two different levels? Explain.
(b) Which body in the table is the judiciary at the same level as the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha?
questions.a: (a) No. Both stand for the level of the whole country, set against the State level in each row; the table simply uses two names for it. (b) The Supreme Court of India.
s: Part (a): both mean the level of the whole country, opposite the State level
Part (b): the Supreme Court of India

questions.q:
Class 6 is building an exhibition model called 'Who makes and judges the laws for the people of a typical Indian State'. Their budget is Rs 2,000. The shop's price list: Lok Sabha chamber Rs 450; Rajya Sabha chamber Rs 450; State Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) Rs 400; second State House Rs 400; Supreme Court building Rs 350; High Court building Rs 300.
(a) Which pieces show the bodies that formulate national laws, and what do they cost together?
(b) Which pieces show a State's legislature as the table gives it for most States, and the State-level judiciary, and what do they cost?
(c) After (a) and (b), how much money is left? Can the class buy both the Supreme Court building and a second State House?
(d) The class can add only one more piece. Should it be the Supreme Court building or a second State House? Decide, using (c) and the chapter's table.
questions.a: (a) The Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha chambers: 450 + 450 = Rs 900. (b) One State Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) and the High Court: 400 + 300 = Rs 700. (c) 2,000 - 900 - 700 = Rs 400 left. Both pieces together cost 350 + 400 = Rs 750, more than Rs 400, so only one can be bought (each alone fits). (d) The Supreme Court building. The table puts the Supreme Court of India in the judiciary at the All India level, so it judges for the people of every State, and without it the model shows no court above the State. A second House is found in only a few States, while most States have a single assembly, so for a typical State it would show the exception. (A choice of the second House earns the mark only if it is argued from the few two-House States and admits the model then lacks the All India court.)
s: Part (a): Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, Rs 900
Part (b): Vidhan Sabha and High Court, Rs 700
Part (c): Rs 400 left; Rs 750 for both, so only one
Part (d): the Supreme Court building, since it is the All India court and most States have one assembly

questions.q: A classmate asks, 'Important decisions are made in the High Court, so why isn't it called a House?' Explain, using the chapter's meaning of 'House' and what the judiciary does, why the High Court is not a House but the Vidhan Sabha is.
questions.a: The chapter defines a House as an assembly where laws are discussed or passed; Houses belong to the legislature, which makes, updates or removes laws. The High Court is part of the judiciary, the system of courts that decides whether someone has broken the law and what action should follow, and sometimes whether a law is fair. It judges laws rather than discussing or passing them, so it is not a House. The Vidhan Sabha is the State Assembly where State laws are discussed or passed, so it is a House.
s: A House is an assembly where laws are discussed or passed (legislature)
The High Court is a court of the judiciary that decides cases under the law
The Vidhan Sabha discusses or passes laws, so it is a House

questions.q: Write three short newspaper headlines: (i) one about the judiciary at the State level, (ii) one about the legislature at the national level, each using the chapter's correct name for the body, and (iii) one headline that gets a level wrong, followed by its correction.
questions.a: Any fitting headlines, for example: (i) 'High Court hears case on State water rules'. (ii) 'Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha discuss new national cybercrime law'. (iii) 'Vidhan Sabha passes law for the whole of India' - wrong: national laws are formulated by the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha; the Vidhan Sabha is the State Assembly.
s: (i) A State-level judiciary headline naming the High Court
(ii) A national legislature headline naming the Lok Sabha and/or Rajya Sabha
(iii) A headline with a wrong level and a correct correction

questions.q: True or False? 'A State legislature can have two Houses, just like the national legislature.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter's table.
questions.a: True. The table notes that most States have a single assembly, but a few States have two, so a State legislature can have two Houses, as the national level has the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: most States have one assembly but a few have two

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A law on currency for the whole country is not passed by any State's Vidhan Sabha.
Reason (R): The Vidhan Sabha is a House, an assembly where laws are discussed or passed.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. A is true because national laws are formulated by the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, while the Vidhan Sabha is the State Assembly at the State level. R is true too, but being a House does not explain A: if anything it says the Vidhan Sabha does pass laws. What explains A is the level, not whether the body is a House.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A student's revision card places five bodies:
(1) Lok Sabha: legislature, national level
(2) High Court: judiciary, All India level
(3) Vidhan Sabha: legislature, State level
(4) Supreme Court of India: judiciary, State level
(5) Rajya Sabha: legislature, State level
Evaluate each placement against the chapter's table, correct every wrong one, and say what single mix-up explains entries (2) and (4).
questions.a: (1) Correct: the Lok Sabha is one of the two Houses at the national level. (2) Wrong: the High Court is the judiciary at the State level. (3) Correct: the Vidhan Sabha is the State Assembly. (4) Wrong: the Supreme Court of India is at the All India level. (5) Wrong: the Rajya Sabha is a House at the national level, with the Lok Sabha. Entries (2) and (4) come from one mix-up: the student has swapped the levels of the two courts.
s: (1) Lok Sabha judged correct
(2) High Court corrected to State level
(3) Vidhan Sabha judged correct
(4) Supreme Court corrected to All India level, with the swap of the two courts named
(5) Rajya Sabha corrected to national level

questions.q: A reporter wants an answer from the executive head of the government whose list in the chapter's table covers Agriculture in her State. Whom should she ask?
questions.a: The Chief Minister of the State
o: The Chief Minister of the State
The Governor, as head of the State
The Prime Minister of the country
The President of India

questions.q:
Read the statements about the executive in the chapter's table.
1. The Chief Minister is the executive head of a State.
2. Public health appears on the Central government's list of functions.
3. Inter-state commerce appears on the State government's list of functions.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only. Statement 2 is wrong: Public health is on the State government's list. Statement 3 is wrong: Inter-state Commerce is on the Central government's list.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
(a) The Central government makes a new national law on food safety. Which function on the State list in the chapter's table comes into play when this law is to be put into effect in a State?
(b) Explain, using this example, how the Central and State executives work together.
questions.a: (a) Adaptation and implementation of laws made by the Central government at the State level. (b) The Central government makes the law for the whole country; the State executive adjusts it to suit the State and puts it into effect there, for example through its own officials checking food shops. One level makes the national law, the other carries it out in the State.
s: Part (a): adaptation and implementation of Central laws at the State level
Part (b): the Centre makes the law; the State adapts and carries it out

questions.q: A student's chart says: 'Fisheries appear on neither list in the chapter's table, so fisheries are not a matter for any government in India.' What is wrong with her conclusion?
questions.a: The table's list of functions is not exhaustive
o: The table's list of functions is not exhaustive
Fisheries come under Defence on the Central list
Fisheries are on both lists, in the same way as Education
Only the judiciary deals with matters left off the lists

questions.q: Two pupils argue: one says Education is purely a Central matter, the other that it is purely a State matter. Show, using the chapter's table, that neither 'purely' can be right, and say what this tells you about how the two lists are related.
questions.a: Education appears in the Central government's list of functions and also in the State government's list, so it cannot belong purely to one of them; both pupils are half right and both 'purely' claims fail. This shows the two lists are not completely separate: some functions are shared by the Central and State executives (and the lists are not exhaustive).
s: Education is on the Central list
Education is also on the State list, so neither 'purely' holds
The lists overlap; some functions are shared

questions.q:
A water-borne disease breaks out in 30 villages of a State. 1,200 patients have been admitted to the district hospitals, which have 1,500 beds, and the doctors already on duty can look after the patients admitted so far. Of the 150 new cases in the last three days, 120 came from villages that drink from one polluted canal. The State needs medicines for the patients, police to manage crowds at clinics, and clean water released into the canal. A reporter asks why the Governor is not personally running the response.
(a) Under which three functions on the State list in the chapter's table do these needs fall?
(b) How should the Governor's office answer the reporter, and who leads the response instead?
(c) How many hospital beds are still free, and what share of the new cases came from the canal villages?
(d) The Chief Minister's office has money for only one new cell this week: a Public Health Cell to hire more doctors, or an Irrigation Cell to clean and refill the canal. Which should it choose? Justify using (c).
questions.a: (a) Public health (medicines for patients), police, law and order (crowds) and irrigation (canal water). (b) The Governor is the nominal head of the State: not the actual executive head, and normally does not interfere in the affairs of the State government; the response is led by the Chief Minister, the executive head. (c) 1,500 - 1,200 = 300 beds free; 120 of 150 new cases, that is 80%, came from the canal villages. (d) The Irrigation Cell. Both are State functions, but the doctors on duty are coping and 300 beds are still free, while 4 out of 5 new cases come from the polluted canal; cleaning the canal stops new cases at their source. (A Public Health Cell earns the mark if it is justified from (c): about 150 / 3 = 50 new cases a day would fill the 300 free beds in about 6 days, so more doctors may soon be needed.)
s: Part (a): public health, police and law and order, irrigation
Part (b): Governor is a nominal head who normally does not interfere; the CM leads
Part (c): 300 beds free; 120 of 150, or 80%, from canal villages
Part (d): a cell chosen and justified from (c): the canal source (80%) or beds filling at about 50 a day

questions.q:
In one week a State faces a shortage of coins in its markets and a breakdown of mobile phone networks.
