(a) Going by the chapter's table, which government's list covers both of these matters, and under which functions?
(b) Should the State's Chief Minister or the Prime Minister's government be the one to act on them? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The Central government's list: Currency (coins) and Communications (phone networks). (b) The Prime Minister's government, because these are Central functions and the Prime Minister is the executive head of the Central government; the Chief Minister heads the State executive, whose list does not include them.
s: Part (a): Central list, Currency and Communications
Part (b): the PM's government, as executive head of the Centre

questions.q: Riya argues: 'Defence is a function of the Central government, and the Prime Minister is its executive head, so the Prime Minister must be the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces.' What does the chapter's table say?
questions.a: The President of India holds that title. The table names the President of India as the nominal head and Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces; the Prime Minister is the executive head, so being the executive head of the government that handles Defence does not make him Supreme Commander.
o: The President of India holds that title
The Prime Minister holds it, just as Riya says
The President and the Prime Minister share it
The PM holds it, since Defence is a Central function

questions.q: Arun claims: 'Trade between two States is a matter for those two State governments alone, since agriculture and police are already on each State's own list.' Check his claim against the chapter's table.
questions.a: No. Agriculture and police, law and order are indeed on the State government's list, but the table puts Inter-state Commerce, trade between States, on the Central government's list. So trade between two States is not left to the two State governments alone; what is on a State's list does not decide a matter the table gives to the Centre.
s: Verdict: No
Agriculture and police are State functions, as he says
Inter-state Commerce is on the Central list, so his conclusion fails

questions.q: A State's budget speech promises four new projects. Going by the chapter's table, which project would be out of place, because its function is on the Central government's list and not on the State's?
questions.a: A new atomic energy plant run by the State
o: A new atomic energy plant run by the State
New canals to bring water to farms in dry areas
More doctors for district hospitals
Better seeds and training for farmers

questions.q:
Your grandmother dealt with the government three times this year: (1) she reported a theft at the police station, (2) she was treated at a government district hospital during a fever outbreak handled under public health, and (3) she had to exchange old currency notes that had been withdrawn across the country.
(a) Going by the chapter's table, on whose list of functions does each dealing fall?
(b) Which executive head leads the government she dealt with most often this year?
questions.a: (a) (1) Police, law and order: the State government's list. (2) Public health: the State government's list. (3) Currency: the Central government's list. (b) The State government, two of her three dealings, so its executive head, the Chief Minister.
s: Part (a): police and public health on the State list; currency on the Central list
Part (b): the State government (2 of 3), led by the Chief Minister

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's table, Irrigation is a function of the Central government.
Reason (R): Agriculture and Irrigation both appear on the State government's list of functions.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Irrigation is on the State government's list, together with Agriculture, Public health and others; it is not on the Central government's list. So R is true and A is false.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
A play about the executive has four characters. Match each role in Column A with the office in Column B, going by the chapter's table.
Column A: 1. Nominal head of a State  2. Executive head of the government whose list includes Irrigation  3. Executive head of the government whose list includes Currency  4. Nominal head of the country
Column B: a. Governor  b. Chief Minister  c. Prime Minister  d. President of India
questions.a: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d. Irrigation is on the State list, so its government is led by the Chief Minister as executive head, with the Governor as nominal head; Currency is on the Central list, so its government is led by the Prime Minister as executive head, with the President of India as nominal head.

questions.q:
A newspaper's 'Who does what?' column lists six tasks:
T1 printing new currency notes; T2 police patrols on city roads; T3 a programme to improve public health in hospitals; T4 talks with another country about a border; T5 supplying canal water to farms; T6 a scheme to train school teachers.
A reader then writes: 'Tourism is on neither list in the chapter's table, so it must be a job for the Central government.'
(a) Which of the six tasks belong only to the Central government's list in the chapter's table?
(b) Which belong only to the State government's list?
(c) Which task could belong to either list? Explain.
(d) Is the reader's conclusion about tourism justified? Use what the chapter says about its lists.
questions.a: (a) T1 (currency) and T4 (foreign affairs). (b) T2 (police, law and order), T3 (public health) and T5 (irrigation). (c) T6 (education): Education appears in both the Central and the State lists. (d) No. The chapter says its list of functions is not exhaustive, so a task missing from both lists tells us nothing about which government handles it; it cannot be handed to the Centre just because it is missing.
s: Part (a): T1 and T4
Part (b): T2, T3 and T5
Part (c): T6, as Education is on both lists
Part (d): not justified; the lists are not exhaustive, so a missing task points to neither government

questions.q:
During a festival, a city needs police to manage huge crowds, and a hospital needs more doctors for the injured.
(a) Under which two functions on the State list in the chapter's table do these needs fall?
(b) A student says the Prime Minister's government must handle both, because the Prime Minister is the executive head of India. Correct him.
questions.a: (a) Police, law and order; and public health. (b) Both functions are on the State government's list, so they are handled by the State government, whose executive head is the Chief Minister. The Prime Minister is the executive head of the Central government, whose list includes matters such as Defence and Currency.
s: Part (a): police, law and order; public health
Part (b): State functions, led by the Chief Minister, not the PM

questions.q: The chapter's table calls the President the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces and also a nominal head. A student thinks these two facts contradict each other. Explain, using the glossary, how both can be true.
questions.a: The table gives the President both titles. 'Nominal' means in name only: the President is not the actual executive head and normally does not interfere in the affairs of the Central government, although the President does have certain powers under special circumstances. So the President can hold the title of Supreme Commander while the actual executive head is the Prime Minister. There is no contradiction: one is a title, the other describes how far the President actually runs the government.
s: Nominal means in name only; not the actual executive head
The President normally does not interfere but has certain powers in special circumstances
Both can hold: a title versus who actually runs the executive (the Prime Minister)

questions.q: A State government orders all its village councils to hold an open meeting every month. A villager says only the Central government can give such an order, because it handles the Formulation of National Policies. Which correction fits the chapter's table?
questions.a: Local government is on the State's own list
o: Local government is on the State's own list
Police, law and order lets any State do it
The Centre's list covers it under Education
No list covers it, so no government may do it

questions.q:
A school magazine article on 'How India's executive works' makes five statements:
(1) 'The Prime Minister is the nominal head of India.'
(2) 'In a State, the Governor runs the government as its executive head.'
(3) 'Adapting Central laws for use in a State is the Prime Minister's job.'
(4) 'Police, law and order is a function of the State government.'
(5) 'Atomic energy is looked after by each State government.'
Evaluate each statement against the chapter's table and rewrite every wrong one correctly.
questions.a: (1) Wrong: the President of India is the nominal head; the Prime Minister is the executive head of the Central government. (2) Wrong: the Governor is the nominal head; the Chief Minister is the executive head of the State. (3) Wrong: adaptation and implementation of laws made by the Central government at the State level is on the State government's list. (4) Correct: police, law and order is on the State list. (5) Wrong: Atomic Energy is on the Central government's list.
s: (1) Judged wrong and rewritten: President nominal, PM executive head
(2) Judged wrong and rewritten: Governor nominal, CM executive head
(3) Judged wrong and rewritten: adapting Central laws is a State function
(4) Judged correct
(5) Judged wrong and rewritten: Atomic Energy is a Central function

questions.q: A student writes: 'A nominal head is unimportant; the post is only a name.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter's glossary, its table and its account of Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam. Cover (i) what 'nominal' means in the chapter, (ii) who holds the actual executive power at the Centre, (iii) what the glossary says a nominal head still has, (iv) how Dr Kalam's time as President shows influence without running the government, and (v) your judgement of the claim.
questions.a: (i) Nominal means 'in name only': the President of India and the Governor of a State are not the actual executive heads and normally do not interfere in the affairs of the Central or State government. (ii) The Prime Minister, the executive head of the Central government. (iii) Certain powers under special circumstances, so the post is not empty. (iv) Dr Kalam, the 11th President (2002 to 2007), remained deeply connected to the people, especially the youth, through his passion for good education and innovation, and encouraged young Indians to dream big and work hard; the chapter says that though his position was nominal he could play an important role, impacting countless lives. (v) The claim is wrong: a nominal head does not run the government, but has certain powers in special circumstances and, as Dr Kalam showed, can have a real influence on people.
s: (i) Nominal means in name only; not the actual executive head
(ii) The Prime Minister holds actual executive power
(iii) Certain powers under special circumstances
(iv) Kalam's connection with youth and education, impacting countless lives
(v) Judgement: the claim fails; nominal is not the same as unimportant

questions.q: True or False? 'Defence is on the Central government's list, so a State government has no role in keeping law and order.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Defence is on the Central government's list, but Police, law and order is on the State government's list. Defence and law and order are different functions, so the State government does keep law and order through its police.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Police, law and order is a State function; Defence is a different, Central function

questions.q: Before deciding the route of a new road through a village, officials hold a meeting where any villager may speak. No vote is taken, but the villagers' views make the officials move the route away from the school. Which idea from the chapter does this show best?
questions.a: Grassroots democracy: ordinary citizens have a say
o: Grassroots democracy: ordinary citizens have a say
Direct democracy: every villager's vote decided the route
Representative democracy: elected MLAs chose the route
Separation of powers between the three organs at work

questions.q:
(a) 'Democracy' comes from dēmos and kratos. Using the meaning of kratos, what would a made-up word 'studentocracy' mean?
(b) If a school of 1,000 students were run as a studentocracy, why would it still probably need student representatives? Use the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Kratos means 'rule' or 'power', so 'studentocracy' would mean rule by the students. (b) Just as all the people cannot actually rule, 1,000 students could not all take every decision or all go to the principal; it would not be practical, so they would elect representatives to speak and decide for them.
s: Part (a): rule (or power) of the students, from kratos
Part (b): not practical for all to decide, so representatives are elected

questions.q: The 20 families of a small residents' group must fix a date for their Diwali get-together. Going by the chapter's reasoning about when representatives are needed, which method fits best?
questions.a: All 20 families vote directly on the date
o: All 20 families vote directly on the date
They elect 5 representatives to choose for them
The secretary alone fixes it, since votes waste time
They wait for their MLA to decide it in the Assembly

questions.q: A class has no monitor. It wants to ask the principal to change the date of a field trip. Going by the chapter, what is the practical way to do it?
questions.a: Pick one representative just for this request
o: Pick one representative just for this request
The whole class must go, since it has no monitor
Wait until a monitor is elected for the whole year
Ask the local MLA to take the request to the principal

questions.q:
Read the statements about democracy in the chapter.
1. A country whose citizens elect MLAs and MPs to decide on laws is a direct democracy.
2. A class that elects a monitor to speak to the principal follows the same principle as citizens electing MLAs.
3. In principle, a 17-year-old Indian citizen has the right to vote in India's elections.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only. Statement 2 is correct: the chapter says it is the same principle at the State or national levels, where people vote for representatives. Statement 1 is wrong: electing MLAs and MPs makes India a representative democracy. Statement 3 is wrong: in principle, citizens above the age of 18 have the right to take part in elections.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
The school football club has 40 members in 5 age teams of 8, and must choose a jersey colour. After a long discussion fails to settle it, the coach calls a vote by raised hands. On the day, 2 members are absent; 17 raise hands for blue and all the other members present raise hands for red. Next, the club wants to ask the principal for more ground time. Lunch break is 30 minutes, and the principal's office has 6 chairs, one of them the principal's.
(a) What kind of democracy is the jersey vote, according to the chapter, and why?
(b) The 2 absent members say they would have voted blue. Could their votes have changed the result? Show the numbers.
(c) Some members suggest that each age team picks one member to go to the principal. What kind of democracy is this, and what is its counterpart at the national level in India?
(d) Should the club send a single representative or the 5 team representatives? Decide, using the details given and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Direct democracy: each member present gave his or her own opinion by raising hands, and the option with the larger number of hands was chosen. (b) 40 - 2 = 38 present; red got 38 - 17 = 21. With the absent members, blue would have had 17 + 2 = 19, still fewer than 21, so the result would not change. (c) Representative democracy: members choose people to speak for them; at the national level, people elect MPs (Members of Parliament). (d) Either choice earns the mark if it is justified. One representative: the chapter says it is enough to send a representative, and one person can make the request quickly within a 30-minute break. Five representatives: they fit in the 5 free chairs, and each age team's need for ground time is carried by someone it chose. Sending all 40 is not an option: it would not be practical, as the chapter's class example shows.
s: Part (a): direct democracy, every member present voting
Part (b): no; blue 19 against red 21
Part (c): representative democracy; MPs at the national level
Part (d): one or five representatives, justified from the chairs, the time or the chapter

questions.q: Meena, aged 25, and her brother Arjun, aged 17, are Indian citizens. An election for their State Assembly and an election at the national level are both due. Going by the chapter, which statement fits?
questions.a: Meena may vote for an MLA and an MP; Arjun may not yet
o: Meena may vote for an MLA and an MP; Arjun may not yet
Both may vote for an MLA, but only Meena may vote for an MP
Meena may vote for an MP only, as the MPs choose the MLAs
Both may vote in both, as every citizen may vote in principle

questions.q:
(a) A class of 36 decides the date of a field trip by raised hands: 20 hands go up for Friday and the rest for Saturday. Which date wins, and by how many hands?
(b) Why could the same method not be used to choose every law for a State with crores of people? Use the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Saturday gets 36 - 20 = 16 hands, so Friday wins by 20 - 16 = 4 hands. (b) It is not possible or practical for all the people of a State to take every decision directly; so, through elections, people vote for representatives (MLAs) who discuss laws in the Assembly.
s: Part (a): Friday wins by 4 hands (20 to 16)
Part (b): not practical for all to decide; representatives (MLAs) are elected

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When all 30 members of a chess club vote by raising hands to fix their meeting day, it is direct democracy.
Reason (R): In a vote by raised hands, the decision goes to whichever option gets the larger number of hands.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. A is true: every member's own opinion is taken, which the chapter calls direct democracy. R is true: that is how the chapter describes voting. But R only says how the winner is found; elected representatives can also decide by the larger number. What makes the club's vote direct is that every member votes for himself or herself.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Dev says: 'In India, democracy works only through elected representatives. Ordinary citizens have no part in decisions except casting a vote.' How far is he right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. It is true that India is a representative democracy: at the State and national levels, people vote for MLAs and MPs who discuss laws and decide in the assemblies. But the chapter also describes grassroots democracy, a system that enables and encourages the participation of ordinary citizens at the base of the pyramid, so that citizens can have a say in decisions that affect them. So ordinary citizens are meant to do more than vote.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: representative democracy through MLAs and MPs
Wrong part: grassroots democracy gives ordinary citizens a say in decisions affecting them

questions.q:
A school committee of 6 elected class representatives must choose a trip: 4 want a museum and 2 want a zoo. Instead of voting at once, they discuss the cost and the distance for 20 minutes, and one zoo supporter changes her mind.
(a) How many representatives now favour the museum, and what does the chapter call the way they settled their different opinions?
(b) How is this decision different from the chapter's class picnic vote?
questions.a: (a) 4 + 1 = 5 favour the museum and 1 the zoo. The chapter calls it dialogue and debate: representatives discuss problems and solutions and try to convince each other whenever there are different opinions. (b) In the picnic vote every student's own opinion was taken by raised hands, which is direct democracy; here elected representatives decide for their classes after discussion, which is representative democracy.
s: Part (a): 5 for the museum; dialogue and debate
Part (b): picnic vote was direct (every student); this is representatives deciding (representative democracy)

questions.q: A student makes a poster on India's 2024 elections using the Indian number system. The chapter gives some 970 million voters. Which figure should the poster show?
questions.a: About 97 crore voters
o: About 97 crore voters
About 9.7 crore voters
About 970 crore voters

questions.q: True or False? 'A 15-year-old class monitor, elected by her class, has no part in any kind of democracy, because only citizens above 18 have the right to vote in India's elections.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The age of 18 applies to the State and national elections, but the chapter treats a class electing its monitor or class representative as the same principle as people electing MLAs and MPs: a small representative democracy. So the monitor is part of a democratic process in her class.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: electing a class monitor is itself representative democracy; the age rule is for State and national elections

questions.q:
A housing colony in Kochi has 300 families living in 12 blocks of equal size. Each block chooses one representative, and the 12 representatives meet the builder whenever there is a problem. Now the colony must choose between two dates for its annual festival, with one adult voting for each family. The association hall holds 150 people, the decision is needed within a week, and the hall is free on two evenings that week.
(a) How many families does each block representative speak for, and how many evening sessions in the hall would it take for one adult from every family to vote in person?
(b) Why does the colony send representatives to the builder instead of all 300 families? Use the chapter's class example.
(c) At the builder's last visit, 9 of the 12 representatives agreed to his plan. Does that mean every one of the families they speak for agreed? Show the number of families and explain.
(d) For the festival date, should the colony hold a vote of all 300 families, or let the 12 representatives vote after asking their blocks? Decide, using (a) and the chapter's meaning of direct democracy.
questions.a: (a) 300 / 12 = 25 families per representative; 300 / 150 = 2 evening sessions, which fit in the two free evenings. (b) Just as it is not practical for a whole class to go to the principal, so the class sends its representative, it is not practical for 300 families to meet the builder; the representatives carry their views. (c) No. The 9 representatives speak for 9 x 25 = 225 families, but in representative democracy the representatives decide on the families' behalf; the opinion of each family was not taken one by one, as it would be in direct democracy, so some of those 225 families may have disagreed. (d) A vote of all 300 families. The representatives' vote would be quicker, but here a direct vote is practical: two sessions of 150 fit in the week, and in direct democracy every family's own opinion is taken. The chapter turns to representatives when it is not practical for everyone to take part, which is not the case for this decision.
s: Part (a): 25 families; 2 sessions
Part (b): not practical for all, like the class sending a representative
Part (c): no; 225 families, but representatives decide on their behalf, so not every family's view was taken
Part (d): a direct vote, since 2 sessions fit in the week (accept the representatives only if the answer shows a cost the stem gives)

questions.q: A student says, 'India is a representative democracy only because it is so big; a modern democracy with fewer people would be a direct democracy.' Which line of the chapter goes against her?
questions.a: Like any modern democracy, India is representative
o: Like any modern democracy, India is representative
India is the world's largest democracy, with 970 million voters
In principle, all Indian citizens above 18 have the right to vote
The class picnic vote was a case of direct democracy

questions.q: Create two short school situations that are different from the chapter's own picnic and class-monitor examples: one that shows direct democracy and one that shows representative democracy. For each, say what makes it that kind of democracy.
questions.a: Any two fitting situations, for example: Direct: the 30 members of the school's chess club all vote by raising hands to choose the day for their weekly meeting; every member's opinion is taken and the larger number wins. Representative: each class elects one student to a school committee, and the committee members meet the principal to discuss the canteen menu; the students are represented by people they chose because it is not practical for everyone to meet the principal.
s: A new direct-democracy situation in which everyone votes
A new representative-democracy situation with elected representatives
The feature that makes each one direct or representative is explained

questions.q: Compare and analyse direct democracy and representative democracy under these headings: (i) what each means, (ii) one example of each from school life, other than a class picnic vote or a class monitor, (iii) who actually takes the decision, (iv) when each is practical, and (v) which one India's elections for MLAs and MPs follow, and why.
questions.a: (i) In direct democracy every person's own opinion is taken on the decision; in representative democracy people elect representatives who decide on their behalf. (ii) Any fitting pair, for example: direct, the members of a school club all voting by raised hands on their meeting day; representative, each class electing one student to a school committee that meets the principal. (iii) Direct: all the members together, the option with more votes winning; representative: the elected representatives, after discussion. (iv) Direct works when everyone can practically take part, as in one small group; representative is needed when it is not practical for everyone to take part, as with a whole class going to the principal, or a whole State or country. (v) Representative democracy: citizens above 18 vote for MLAs at the State level and MPs at the national level, because it is not possible for all the people to rule directly.
s: (i) Meanings of both
(ii) A new school example of each
(iii) Who decides in each
(iv) When each is practical
(v) India: representative, because all cannot rule directly

questions.q: Zoya claims: 'Our housing society's show-of-hands vote on park timings and the election of MLAs are both democratic, even though only one of them is direct democracy.' Is she right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. Democracy means rule of the people. The show-of-hands vote is direct democracy: every member's opinion is taken and the larger number of hands decides. Electing MLAs is representative democracy: people vote in elections for representatives who discuss laws in the State Assembly. Both let the people decide, directly or through those they elect, so both are democratic, and only the society's vote is direct.
s: Verdict: Yes
Society vote: direct democracy, every opinion taken
MLA election: representative democracy; both are rule of the people

questions.q:
Read this report from a State newspaper.
'In the State Assembly yesterday, members elected from every part of the State discussed a proposed law to control the price of water from tankers. Some members wanted a strict price limit; others warned that tanker owners might stop supplying villages. The debate went on for six hours. By the end, several members who had opposed the limit agreed to a milder version, and the law was passed.'
(a) Which organ of government is at work here, and what are its elected members at the State level called?
(b) What does the chapter call the way such members settle different opinions, and which line of the report shows it working?
(c) Why is the law decided by these members and not by a vote of every citizen of the State?
(d) A member complains that the six hours were wasted and that the strict price limit first proposed should have been passed at once. Weigh the time against what the report shows the debate achieved, and give your judgement.
questions.a: (a) The legislature, the organ that makes laws through an assembly of representatives; its members at the State level are Members of Legislative Assembly (MLAs). (b) Dialogue and debate: members discuss laws, problems and solutions and try to convince each other; the line 'several members who had opposed the limit agreed to a milder version' shows it working. (c) It is not possible or practical for all the people to rule directly, so they elect representatives to discuss and decide for them; India is a representative democracy. (d) Six hours is a real cost, but the debate was worth it. The chapter says members discuss laws, problems and solutions and, through dialogue and debate, try to convince each other when opinions differ. Here the debate brought out the risk that tanker owners might stop supplying villages, and the law was changed to a milder version that opponents could accept; passing the strict limit at once would have ignored that risk. (A judgement for speed earns the mark only if it answers the supply risk raised in the debate.)
s: Part (a): the legislature; MLAs
Part (b): dialogue and debate, with the line where opponents agreed
Part (c): not practical for all to rule, so representatives decide
Part (d): weighs six hours against the supply risk the debate brought out, with a judgement

questions.q: A school of 1,200 students wants students to have a real say in two decisions: choosing one of two themes for Annual Day, and asking the principal to repair the playground. Design a plan for both decisions. Your plan must (i) say which decision should use direct democracy and how, (ii) say which should use representatives and how they are chosen, (iii) give the chapter's reason for each choice, (iv) say how the representatives should handle disagreement among themselves, and (v) explain how the plan reflects grassroots democracy.
questions.a: Any plan that meets all five, for example: (i) Annual Day theme: every student votes in class by raised hands or slips, and the theme with more votes across the school wins; every student's opinion is taken. (ii) Playground: each class elects one representative, and two of them are chosen to meet the principal. (iii) A vote by everyone is practical for a simple choice between two themes, as in the chapter's class vote; but it is not practical for 1,200 students to go to the principal, so, as the chapter says, it is enough to send a representative. (iv) The representatives discuss the problem and possible solutions and, through dialogue and debate, try to convince each other when opinions differ. (v) Ordinary students, not only the head boy or girl, have a say in decisions that affect them, which is what the chapter calls grassroots democracy.
s: (i) Direct vote for the theme, with how it is done
(ii) Elected representatives for the playground request
(iii) Chapter reasons: direct where practical, representatives where all cannot go
(iv) Dialogue and debate among representatives
(v) Ordinary students having a say: grassroots democracy

questions.q: True or False? 'India is the world's largest democracy because every one of its citizens has the right to vote.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. In principle only Indian citizens above the age of 18 have the right to take part in elections, not every citizen. The chapter calls India the world's largest democracy because it had some 970 million voters in 2024.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: only citizens above 18 may vote; India is the largest democracy with about 970 million voters
